43.title: The sower (Matthew 13:1–23)
43.hook: seed on the path, the rocks, the thorns, and the good ground
43.tomorrow: the mustard seed and the yeast
43.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the sower at Sunday Mass and some use its four kinds of ground to examine their hearts in prayer or before confession.

segments.voice: Last week ended with the storm, and three words to the sea: peace, be still. Did you breathe through a worry? Day forty-three. A new week: the stories he told.

The same lake, a calmer day. So many people have come to hear Jesus that he gets into a boat, pushes out a little, and sits down to teach, while the whole crowd stands on the shore. And instead of a lecture, he tells a story about farming. It's a story from the fields around that lake. In the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the sower went forth to sow." A man walks across a field, scattering seed by the handful. Some falls on the path. Some on rocky ground. Some among thorns. And some on good ground. That's almost the whole story. Today's word is the kind of story it is.
screen: `A BOAT FOR A PULPIT.` → `A SOWER GOES OUT TO SOW.` → `FOUR KINDS OF GROUND.`

segments.voice: The word is parable. In Greek, parabolē: para, beside, and ballein, to throw. A story thrown down beside something, so you can compare them. An everyday picture laid next to the kingdom of God. And a parable doesn't explain itself. It ends, and you're left holding it. Jesus finishes this one with a line: "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." Now the four grounds. The seed on the path gets snatched by birds before it can sink in. The seed on rocks springs up fast, because the soil is shallow, and then withers in the sun, no roots. The seed among thorns grows, but the thorns grow too, and choke it. And the seed on good ground bears fruit: some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. Later, his disciples ask what it means, and Matthew gives Jesus's explanation. The seed is the word of the kingdom. The path is someone who hears it and doesn't understand, and it's taken away. The rocks are someone who receives it with joy, but when trouble comes, they fall away. The thorns are the cares of the world and the lure of riches, choking it. The good ground is the one who hears, understands, and bears fruit. Notice something about the sower. He's not careful. He throws seed everywhere, even on the path, even on the rocks. Seed costs something, and he's generous with it anyway. Some readers say a single person can be all four grounds, on different days. Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass, and some use it to examine their hearts.
screen: `PARABOLĒ — THROWN BESIDE.` · `THE PATH, THE ROCKS, THE THORNS.` · `GOOD GROUND: A HUNDREDFOLD.` · `A SOWER WHO THROWS EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `HE THAT HATH EARS TO HEAR, LET HIM HEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask what kind of ground you are today. Settle and breathe. No judging. Just look. Are you the path today, so hurried that nothing sinks in? The rocks, excited about something good but not rooted? The thorns, so full of worry and wanting that there's no room? Or is there a patch of good ground somewhere, soft and open? There may be some of each. Find the good patch, however small, and rest there. If you pray, you can ask God to make your ground good. The bell holds the time.
Parable. From the Greek for thrown beside: an everyday story laid next to the kingdom of God. Today's word.
Your line: be good ground. Today, when something good is said to you, slow down long enough to let it sink in. Day forty-three.

44.title: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)
44.hook: the kingdom starts smaller than you'd notice and works through everything
44.howItsDone: Catholics hear these parables at Sunday Mass in summer, and many take up Saint Thérèse of Lisieux's little way, doing small daily tasks with great love as a path of holiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower, and our first parable: seed on the path, the rocks, the thorns, the good ground. Your line was be good ground. What kind of ground were you? Day forty-four. Two more seeds today, very small ones.

Hold a mustard seed on your fingertip and you'll barely see it. Drop it on the kitchen floor and you'll never find it again. Then there's a small lump of yeast, a spoonful of old dough from yesterday's bread. You wouldn't look at either one twice. And that's what Jesus reaches for to say what the kingdom of heaven is like. Not a palace. Not an army. Not a thunderclap. A seed you could lose, and a bit of dough a woman hides in the flour. Today: two parables, three verses between them.
screen: `A SEED YOU COULD LOSE.` → `A SPOONFUL OF OLD DOUGH.` → `THIS IS WHAT THE KINGDOM IS LIKE?`

segments.voice: The first, in the Douay-Rheims: "The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field." The least of all the seeds, Jesus says, but when it's grown it becomes a tree, and the birds of the air come and live in its branches. Some scholars point out that mustard is also a bit of a weed: once it's in your field, it spreads. On that reading, the kingdom isn't neat. It takes over. Then the second parable, just one sentence long: "The kingdom of heaven is like to leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened." Leaven is yeast, but not the packet kind. It was a lump of old, sour dough kept back from the last batch. And look at the verb: she hid it. You can't see it working. And three measures of meal, some readers reckon, is enough to bake bread for a crowd. One small hidden lump, and the whole mass rises. Two pictures, one idea. In these parables, the kingdom starts too small to notice, works out of sight, and goes all the way through. Catholics have a saint known for this. Thérèse of Lisieux, a young Carmelite nun, called her path the little way: doing ordinary, tiny things with great love. The Church later named her a Doctor of the Church.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one tiny good thing. Settle and breathe. Let your day come to mind, hour by hour. Somewhere in it is a place for something very small: a kind word to the person at the register, a text that says thinking of you, a cup put away that isn't yours. Not a project. A seed. Pick one. See yourself doing it. It won't look like much. It isn't supposed to. If you pray, you can offer it to God in advance. The bell holds the time.
leaven. An old lump of sour dough, hidden in the flour until the whole batch rises, the kingdom's small, hidden work.
Your line: small is how it starts. Today, do the one tiny good thing, and don't wait to see what it grows into. Day forty-four.

45.title: The good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37)
45.hook: a priest and a Levite pass by, and the despised foreigner stops
45.tomorrow: the lost sheep and the lost coin
45.howItsDone: Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass and in teaching on the works of mercy; Pope Francis's encyclical Fratelli Tutti gives a chapter to it, and some Catholic hospitals and charities take the Samaritan as their model.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mustard seed and the leaven, the yeast hidden in the dough. Your line was small is how it starts. What tiny good thing did you plant? Day forty-five.

A scholar of the Law stands up to test Jesus. What must I do to have eternal life? Jesus turns it back: what does the Law say? And the man answers well: love God with all your heart, soul, strength and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. Right, says Jesus. Do this, and you'll live. But the man wants to pin it down. He wants to know where the edges are. In the Douay-Rheims: "And who is my neighbour?" Who counts, and who doesn't? It's a question about where love is allowed to stop. And Jesus doesn't give him a definition. He tells him a story. Today: the story he tells instead.
screen: `WHAT MUST I DO?` → `LOVE GOD, LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR.` → `AND WHO IS MY NEIGHBOR?`

segments.voice: A man is going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. The road goes down through lonely country, and on it he falls among robbers. He's stripped, beaten and left half dead. A priest comes down the road, sees him, and passes by on the other side. A Levite, who served in the Temple, does the same. The story never says why. People have guessed for centuries, but Jesus doesn't tell us, and he doesn't need to. Then a Samaritan comes. To the people listening, a Samaritan was a neighbor from across a long and bitter religious divide. And this one, Luke says, is moved with compassion. The Greek word comes from the gut, a feeling in your insides. He goes to the man, pours oil and wine on his wounds, bandages them, puts him on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and pays for his care. Two pence, the Douay-Rheims says, and a promise to cover anything more. Then Jesus asks the scholar: "Which of these three, in thy opinion, was neighbour to him that fell among the robbers?" Notice what happened. The man asked, who is my neighbor, who do I have to love? Jesus answers a different question: who acted like a neighbor? The scholar doesn't say the word Samaritan. He says: the one who showed him mercy. And Jesus says: "Go, and do thou in like manner." Early Church writers also read the story another way: Christ as the Samaritan, the wounded man as all of us, the inn as the Church. Pope Francis gave a whole chapter of his letter Fratelli Tutti to this road.
screen: `THE ROAD DOWN TO JERICHO.` · `TWO PASS BY. ONE STOPS.` · `MOVED IN HIS GUT.` · `NOT WHO IS, BUT WHO PROVED NEIGHBOR.` · then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for someone today. Settle and breathe. Think about the roads you'll walk today, the hallways, the streets, the feeds. Who's lying by the side of them? Not always bleeding. Sometimes just lonely, or overwhelmed, or ignored. Picture one person you usually pass by on the other side. Now picture stopping. What would it cost you? Ten minutes? A little awkwardness? If you pray, you can ask for the Samaritan's gut-deep compassion. The bell holds the time.
Samaritan. A stranger from across a bitter divide, the one who stopped and showed mercy on the Jericho road.
Your line: who proved neighbor. Today, don't ask who deserves your help. Stop for one person, and be the neighbor. Day forty-five.

46.title: The lost sheep and the lost coin (Luke 15:1–10)
46.hook: a shepherd leaves ninety-nine and a woman sweeps the whole house
46.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 15 at Sunday Mass and often in Lent; the Good Shepherd carrying a sheep is painted on the walls of the Roman catacombs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the good Samaritan stopped on the Jericho road. Your line was who proved neighbor. Who did you stop for? Day forty-six.

You've lost your keys. You're already late. You check your pockets, then your bag, then your pockets again. You lift the couch cushions. You retrace every step. You are not calm, and you are not reasonable, and you are not going anywhere until you find them. Luke fifteen opens with tax collectors and sinners crowding close to hear Jesus, and some Pharisees and scribes grumbling about it. In the Douay-Rheims: "This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." So Jesus answers with three stories about losing something. Today, the first two: a sheep, and a coin.
screen: `YOU'VE LOST YOUR KEYS.` → `HE EATS WITH SINNERS.` → `THREE STORIES OF LOSING.`

segments.voice: First, a shepherd with a hundred sheep. One wanders off. And he leaves the ninety-nine in the wilderness and goes after the lost one until he finds it. On paper, it isn't sensible. Ninety-nine out of a hundred is a fine result. But the shepherd isn't counting that way. And when he finds it, he doesn't scold it or drag it home. He puts it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and calls his friends: "Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost." Early Christians painted that image, a shepherd with a sheep across his shoulders, on the walls of the catacombs in Rome. Then the second story. A woman has ten silver coins, drachmas in Luke's Greek, and she loses one. She lights a lamp, and she sweeps the whole house, searching carefully until she finds it. And she calls her friends and neighbors: rejoice with me. Look at who the seekers are: a shepherd out in the wilderness, and a woman sweeping her floor. Christians read them both as pictures of God. And each story ends the same way: there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. Not polite approval. A party. And notice who does the work. The sheep doesn't find its way home. The coin can't do anything at all. The searching belongs to the one who lost them.
screen: `NINETY-NINE LEFT BEHIND.` · `ON HIS SHOULDERS, REJOICING.` · `A LAMP AND A BROOM.` · `JOY IN HEAVEN OVER ONE.` · then, large: `REJOICE WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for someone who has drifted. Settle and breathe. Think about the people who used to be close and aren't anymore. A friend who stopped showing up. A cousin you haven't heard from. Someone who stepped away from church, or from the group, or from everybody. Don't think about whose fault it was. Just let one face come. Hold them for a minute, gently. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
groat. The old Douay-Rheims word for the coin: one of ten a woman lost, then swept her house to find.
Your line: he goes looking. Today, reach out to the one who drifted. A short message is enough. No lecture. Just: I thought of you. Day forty-six.

47.title: The son who left (Luke 15:11–24)
47.hook: the younger son spends it all, comes to himself, and the father runs down the road
47.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the prodigal son in Lent and often in preparing for confession, where the penitent comes back and receives absolution; John Paul II's encyclical Dives in Misericordia (1980) meditates on it at length.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lost sheep and the lost coin, the groat swept from under the house. Your line was he goes looking. Did you reach out to someone who drifted? Day forty-seven. Today, the third story of losing, and the most famous.

A man has two sons. The younger one comes to him and says: give me my share of the inheritance. Now. Not when you die. Now. In that world, and in most of ours, that's close to saying: I wish you were already gone. And the father does it. He divides his property, and the younger son sells up, packs everything, and leaves for a far country. There he wastes it all, living wildly. Then a famine hits the land. He takes the only job he can find, feeding pigs, and he's so hungry he'd gladly eat what the pigs are eating. Nobody gives him anything. Today: the son who left, and what happened when he turned around.
screen: `GIVE ME MY SHARE. NOW.` → `A FAR COUNTRY, AND A FAMINE.` → `FEEDING PIGS, STARVING.`

segments.voice: Then comes a small phrase with a lot inside it. The Douay-Rheims says: returning to himself. The King James says he came to himself. As if he'd been away from himself, too. He does the math. My father's hired workers have more bread than they need, and I'm dying of hunger. So he writes a speech in his head: "I will arise, and will go to my father." He'll say: I've sinned against heaven and before you. I'm not worthy to be called your son. Make me one of your hired workers. He's not hoping to be a son again. He's hoping for a job. And he starts the long walk home. Now watch the father. "And when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." He saw him a great way off. Which means he'd been watching the road. And he runs. In that culture, a dignified older man didn't run. He'd have to hitch up his robe and show his legs. The father doesn't care. He reaches his son before the son can reach the village. The son starts his speech, and the father doesn't even let him get to the part about the hired workers. Bring the best robe. A ring for his hand. Shoes for his feet. Kill the fatted calf. "Because this my son was dead, and is come to life again: was lost, and is found." Catholics hear this story as the heart of the sacrament of confession: you come with your speech, and the Father runs to meet you. Pope John Paul the Second built a whole letter on mercy around it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one step back toward someone. Settle and breathe. Think of a relationship where there's distance you helped make. Maybe you left. Maybe you said something. Maybe you just went quiet. You don't have to walk the whole road today. Just picture the first step: a message, a call, an honest sentence. If you pray, you can bring your own speech to God and notice that you don't have to finish it. The bell holds the time.
riotously. How the younger son spent everything in the far country, before the hunger and the long walk home.
Your line: the father runs. Today, take one step back toward someone. The story says the distance is shorter than it looks. Day forty-seven.

48.title: The son who stayed (Luke 15:25–32)
48.hook: the older brother won't go into the party, and the father comes out to him too
48.howItsDone: Catholics hear the whole parable of the prodigal son, older brother included, in Lent, and some use it to examine their consciences before confession, asking which son they resemble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the son who left, who had lived riotously, came home, and the father ran down the road. Your line was the father runs. Did you take a step toward someone? Day forty-eight. The story isn't over. There's another son.

The older son has been out in the field all day. Working, like every day. As he comes near the house, he hears music. Dancing. He calls one of the servants over: what's going on? And the servant tells him, happily: your brother's come home, and your father has killed the fatted calf, because he's got him back safe and sound. And the older son stops in the yard. He won't go in. It's the spot where the dutiful one stands, listening to someone else's party. Today: the son who stayed, and the father who came out to him too.
screen: `A LONG DAY IN THE FIELD.` → `MUSIC FROM THE HOUSE.` → `HE WON'T GO IN.`

segments.voice: The father comes out. That's the first surprise. He ran down the road for the younger son, and now he leaves his own party to plead with the older one. Luke says he began to entreat him. And the older son lets it all out. All these years I've served you. I never once disobeyed. And you never gave me so much as a young goat to celebrate with my friends. But when "this thy son" comes back, who wasted your money, you kill the fatted calf for him. Listen to that: this thy son. Not my brother. He doesn't say the word. Then the father answers, and he starts with a word of great tenderness. In the Douay-Rheims: "Son, thou art always with me, and all I have is thine." The Greek word is teknon, child. Not a scolding. My child, you've been with me all along. Everything I have is yours. Some readers hear in it: you never had to earn it. Then the father gives the word back to him. It was right to celebrate, he says, because "this thy brother" was dead, and is alive again; was lost, and is found. Your son, says the older boy. Your brother, says the father. And then the story stops. We never find out whether the older son goes in. Jesus leaves the door open. He was telling this story, remember, to people grumbling that he ate with sinners. The ending is left for them to write, and for anyone listening. Some Catholics pray with Rembrandt's painting of this parable, where the older son stands off to the side, watching.
screen: `THE FATHER COMES OUT AGAIN.` · `THIS THY SON, NOT MY BROTHER.` · `TEKNON — MY CHILD.` · `THE STORY STOPS AT THE DOOR.` · then, large: `ALL I HAVE IS THINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice resentment without feeding it. Settle and breathe. Is there someone you're keeping score with? Someone who got the thing you worked for, or got forgiven too easily? Let the feeling come up. Name it: resentment. Don't argue with it, and don't feed it more reasons. Just notice where it sits in your body. Then let the father's words sit next to it: all I have is yours. If you pray, you can hand God the scorecard. The bell holds the time.
teknon. The tender Greek word, child, the father used for his angry older son, who wouldn't go in to the party.
Your line: all I have is yours. When you catch yourself keeping score today, say it inside, and see if the door opens a little. Day forty-eight.

49.title: The workers hired late (Matthew 20:1–16)
49.hook: those who worked one hour get the same wage as those who worked all day
49.howItsDone: Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass, and the Catechism teaches that grace is a free and undeserved gift from God; some use the story to examine envy before confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the son who stayed, called teknon, child, standing outside the party. Your line was all I have is yours. Did you catch yourself keeping score? Day forty-nine, the last day of the parables week. It ends with a story that sounds unfair.

Dawn in the town square. Men are standing around, waiting to be picked for a day's work, the way day laborers still wait outside hardware stores this morning. A landowner comes and hires some for his vineyard, for a denarius a day; the Douay-Rheims calls it a penny. Mid-morning he comes back and hires more. At noon, more. Mid-afternoon, more. And at the eleventh hour, with the day nearly gone, he finds men still standing there. "Why stand you here all the day idle?" Because no one hired us, they say. Go on, then, he says, into the vineyard. Then evening comes, and it's time to pay. Today: the payday nobody expected.

segments.voice: The landowner tells his steward: pay them, starting with the last ones hired. The eleventh-hour crew steps up and gets a full denarius. A whole day's wage for one hour. Down the line, the dawn crew starts counting. If they got a denarius, we're getting a lot more. Then they get a denarius. Exactly what they agreed to. And they grumble. These last worked one hour, and you've made them equal to us, who bore the burden of the day and the heat. Their complaint sounds fair. The landowner answers one of them: friend, I'm doing you no wrong. Didn't you agree to a denarius? Take what's yours and go. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Or, is it not lawful for me to do what I will? is thy eye evil, because I am good?" Some readers hear envy in that phrase: a look that resents someone else's good luck. The problem isn't that the dawn workers were cheated. They weren't. The problem is that someone else was given a gift. "So shall the last be first, and the first last." The Catholic Church teaches that grace is like this: a free gift, undeserved, not wages earned. The Catechism describes it as favor: help from God that is free and undeserved. Nobody clocks in for it. And this week's stories all say it: a sower throwing seed everywhere, a seed and some yeast, a Samaritan stopping, a sheep and a coin found, two sons and a father who runs, and now a payday that makes no sense on a spreadsheet.

Notice if there's a little sting. If there is, don't scold yourself. Just picture that person's face when they got the good news, and try, for one breath, to be glad with them.
